strengths: The core idea—combining sparse expert routing with nested, slimmable FFNs—is intuitive, useful, and offers finer-grained compute control than changing only the number of activated experts.

The paper is generally clear and well organized. It provides understandable equations, compute–perplexity plots, a useful inference-mode ablation, and experiments spanning three model sizes, several routing configurations, and multiple training-token budgets.

The experiments suggest that multi-width training is stable and that router probabilities contain useful information for allocating expert capacity. The transfer experiment on LAMBADA is also directionally encouraging.

The appendix reports many important architectural and optimization settings, calibration-set size, width range, hardware, and FLOP breakdowns. The paper honestly acknowledges that evaluation is limited to relatively small models trained from scratch.
The work has limited direct ethical risk and may reduce inference compute, although the impact statement is generic.
weaknesses: The central test-time-training method is not technically specified in a sound, reproducible way. Widths are clipped, discretized in increments of 0.05, converted to integer hidden dimensions using ceil, and implemented by tensor slicing. The resulting language-model loss is piecewise constant and non-differentiable with respect to gamma, yet the appendix says gamma is optimized directly using SGD. No relaxation, straight-through estimator, search method, or custom gradient is described. As written, the proposed optimization cannot provide the claimed gradients, undermining the main empirical contribution.

The purported fixed-budget allocation is not budget preserving. Equation 10 ensures that pre-projection widths sum to Gamma, but clipping each width to [w_min,w_max] and discretization change that sum. Figure 11 even includes Gamma=0.3 for top-2 routing although the minimum feasible total width is 2*0.25=0.5. No redistribution or constrained projection algorithm is given, so comparisons described as operating under a fixed budget are not justified by the stated method.

Training comparisons are compute-unequal. MoSE performs a full-width and a randomly sampled-width forward/backward pass for every batch, whereas the MoE baseline apparently receives one pass. The paper compares equal iterations or nominal data tokens without reporting or matching training FLOPs, despite describing the overhead as minimal. Full-width gains may therefore reflect substantially greater training computation or the regularization from the extra pass.

Efficiency is established only through analytical FLOP counts. Per-token, per-expert variable slicing can fragment computation into many small kernels and incur grouping, padding, routing, and memory overhead. No latency, throughput, memory, kernel-utilization, or end-to-end hardware measurements are reported, so claims concerning efficient deployment and latency are unsupported.

The baseline set is insufficient to establish the claimed Pareto dominance. Vanilla MoE is represented mainly by a single full-compute point; there are no compute-matched models trained at smaller expert widths, alternative adaptive-compute or elastic-MoE methods, varying-k baselines, or training-compute-matched MoE controls.

Results appear to be single runs without uncertainty. Several improvements are small, particularly on WSC with only 273 examples, so their reliability cannot be assessed. Some narrative claims are also contradicted by Table 1: TTT is not consistently best—for example, full-width MoSE has better LAMBADA perplexity for GPT2-Small at 15B tokens, and TTT underperforms MoE on GPT2-Standard/3B WSC.

The calibration protocol is ambiguous about separation from evaluation data and tuning per compute budget. Gamma is optimized separately for each budget on OpenWebText, but the exact split, stopping procedure, gradient implementation, calibration cost, and whether hyperparameters were selected using evaluation performance are not adequately documented.

Originality is moderate rather than high: applying nested/slimmable channels to MoE experts is a natural combination of established slimmable-network and MoE ideas. The paper does not provide theoretical analysis or sufficiently strong comparisons with closely related elastic and nested-transformer methods to demonstrate a deeper new principle.

The limitations discussion covers model scale and the need for training from scratch, but omits the most consequential limitations: additional pretraining cost, non-differentiable width selection, failure of projection to preserve budgets, calibration sensitivity, and the possible gap between FLOPs and realized speed. These unresolved soundness and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance despite the promising idea.

strengths: The core idea—combining sparse expert routing with nested, variable-width expert FFNs—is intuitive, relevant to efficient inference, and constitutes a discernible contribution beyond conventional fixed-width MoE execution.

The evaluation covers three model scales, several routing configurations and training budgets, in-domain and out-of-domain perplexity, two zero-shot tasks, inference-mode ablations, and routing-transfer experiments.
The reported FLOP–perplexity plots generally support the narrower empirical claim that router-conditioned width allocation can outperform uniform-width execution within the trained MoSE models.

The paper is mostly readable and visually clear. The appendix reports several useful architectural and optimization settings, and the authors appropriately acknowledge that the experiments are limited to relatively small models trained from scratch.
No material research-ethics issue is apparent; reducing inference computation could have positive resource implications.
weaknesses: The central test-time-training method is not technically specified in a sound or reproducible way. Expert width is implemented by integer tensor slicing, m(w)=ceil(4dw), and the appendix discretizes widths in increments of 0.05. This operation is non-differentiable with respect to width and therefore to gamma, yet gamma is reportedly optimized directly with SGD. The paper provides no continuous mask, relaxation, straight-through estimator, finite-difference method, or other explanation of how nonzero gradients are obtained. This undermines the main learned-allocation results.

The claimed fixed-budget allocation does not generally preserve its budget. Equation 10 makes the pre-projection widths sum to Gamma, but Equation 11 independently clips each width to [w_min,w_max] and optionally discretizes it without redistributing the residual. The executed widths can therefore sum to substantially more or less than Gamma. At Gamma=|S|, any nonuniform allocation forces some requested widths above 1 and clipping reduces actual compute, explaining why the nominal maximum-budget TTT entries can use fewer FLOPs. The method needs a genuine bounded-simplex projection and explicit accounting of discretization.

Training comparisons are not compute controlled. MoSE performs two forward/backward evaluations per minibatch—one full-width and one random-width—whereas the described MoE baseline uses one. With widths sampled from 0.25 to 1, this entails substantial additional training compute. Consequently, the full-width MoSE improvements over MoE in Table 1 cannot be cleanly attributed to the architecture or training objective. Training FLOPs, wall-clock time, and an equal-compute baseline are absent despite claims of minimal overhead.

The evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. Several headline differences are small, while WSC contains only 273 examples, so reported changes correspond to only a handful of predictions. No confidence intervals, variance, or significance analysis is supplied, making claims of consistent improvement too strong.

The work reports theoretical FLOPs rather than latency, throughput, memory traffic, or energy. Per-token, per-expert variable slicing can create irregular kernels and batching difficulties, so FLOP savings do not establish practical efficiency. This is especially important because efficiency and deployment adaptability are the paper's main motivation.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the appendix: there is no code or pseudocode resolving gamma differentiation, clipping and rounding, positivity constraints, initialization, or whether calibration is repeated separately for every budget. Tokenization, data splits, evaluation harness, expert placement, activation choice, dropped-token handling, exact FLOP formula, and random seeds are also missing or ambiguous.

The experimental comparison set is weak. The paper mainly compares against vanilla MoE and internal MoSE inference modes, without controlled comparisons to nested/slimmable transformer methods, post-training structured pruning, or elastic-MoE approaches discussed in related work. Thus the benefit of the particular MoSE construction over plausible alternatives is not established.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the architecture is largely a direct composition of sparse MoE routing and established nested/slimmable FFNs. The potentially more distinctive contribution is learned adaptive allocation, but that is precisely the component whose optimization and budget constraint are unresolved.

Some presentation claims exceed the demonstrated method. Figure 1 says MoSE lets more experts contribute under the same budget, although the principal formulation assigns widths only after a fixed top-k selection. The paper also describes a continuous spectrum despite using a finite width grid, and Equation 3 contains an indexing inconsistency. These issues obscure the exact contribution.

The limitations discussion is honest about model scale but too narrow. It omits the extra training cost, lack of hardware measurements, non-differentiable width selection, budget violation, statistical uncertainty, and possible calibration-distribution dependence. The generic impact statement likewise offers little substantive consideration of environmental or deployment trade-offs. Overall, the paper has a promising concept, but the unresolved optimization and budgeting issues affect its central claims and prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining sparse expert routing with nested, slimmable FFN experts is a simple but useful idea. It gives one checkpoint substantially finer inference-time compute control than conventional fixed-width MoE models.

Empirical promise: Across several model sizes, token budgets, and routing configurations, the reported results consistently favor adaptive widths. The claimed FLOP reductions of roughly 17–36% at comparable perplexity would be practically meaningful if validated.

The evaluation includes in-domain and out-of-domain perplexity, two zero-shot tasks, routing-transfer experiments, inference-mode ablations, learned-width analyses, and a component-wise FLOP breakdown.
Presentation: The motivation, architecture, and high-level training recipe are generally clear, and the figures communicate the proposed compute-quality trade-offs effectively.

The paper candidly identifies its main scope limitation—experiments only reach 1B parameters and require pretraining slimmability from scratch. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the proposed efficiency method.

The purported fixed-budget assignment is not actually budget preserving after independently clipping or discretizing widths: although the pre-projection widths sum to Gamma, the executed widths generally will not. The manuscript neither gives a constrained projection that preserves the sum nor quantifies budget violations, complicating the interpretation and reproduction of comparisons.

The training comparison is insufficiently controlled. MoSE performs two forward/backward evaluations per minibatch—full width and a sampled width—whereas the MoE baseline apparently performs one. Reporting equal raw token counts therefore does not establish equal training compute, and the paper provides neither training FLOPs/wall-clock costs nor a compute-matched baseline. Even the full-width gains in Table 1 may reflect this extra optimization cost.

Statistical evidence is weak: results appear to come from single runs, with no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is especially problematic for WSC's 273 examples and for the small differences between methods on several metrics.

Efficiency is established only using analytical FLOP counts. Per-token, per-expert variable widths can cause batching, kernel-utilization, dispatch, and padding overheads; no latency, throughput, memory, or energy measurements are reported despite claims about deployment efficiency and performance-latency scaling.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: there is no code or artifact statement; the exact FLOP-counting convention, calibration/evaluation split separation, gamma initialization and constraints, number of calibration optimization steps/epochs, discretization rule, and treatment of capacity overflow/dropped tokens are not adequately specified.

The strongest comparisons are mainly against the paper's own uniform-width mode and vanilla MoE. There is no direct empirical comparison with relevant elastic/pruning/nested-transformer or dynamic-computation baselines under matched training and inference budgets, limiting the originality and significance claims.

The limitations and impact discussions are too narrow. They omit the extra pretraining cost, calibration cost and potential calibration-data dependence, hardware inefficiency of irregular widths, uncertainty from single-run experiments, and possible degradation under broader distribution shifts. The generic impact statement also misses the energy/accessibility benefits and deployment trade-offs explicitly motivating the work.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining sparse expert selection with nested, slimmable expert widths is a natural but useful extension of conditional computation. A single model offering many inference operating points could be practically valuable.

The uniform-width results provide credible evidence that nested experts can support reduced-width execution.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering multiple GPT-style scales, expert counts, routing configurations, token budgets, several downstream benchmarks, and continual-pretraining adaptation of DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

The presentation is generally clear. The nested FFN construction and inference modes are easy to understand, and the Pareto plots, FLOP breakdown, routing diagnostics, and runtime measurements are useful.

The results suggest that slimmable experts can preserve full-width performance while supporting reduced-width execution, which would be practically valuable if validated under a reproducible and technically complete protocol.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive issue: the central test-time training procedure is not technically defined in a way that supports SGD. Equations 3–4 implement a width by applying ceil and slicing channels, while Appendix A.2 says widths are discretized in increments of 0.05. Consequently, the language-model loss has no ordinary differentiable path to gamma in Equation 12. The paper does not specify a straight-through estimator, soft masking, relaxation, finite-difference optimization, or any other gradient mechanism. Thus the main TTT results, which drive most claimed Pareto improvements, cannot be reproduced from the stated method.

The budget rule in Equations 10–11 does not preserve the stated budget after independently clipping widths. Values below w_min are increased and values above w_max are reduced without redistribution. This is especially consequential at Gamma=|S|: unequal normalized probabilities necessarily cause clipping at the upper bound and reduce total executed width. The actual FLOP axis mitigates some comparison concerns, but the claimed fixed-budget optimization and interpretation of gamma are mathematically inaccurate.

The training comparison is not compute-matched. Every MoSE batch receives a full-width pass plus a randomly sampled-width pass, whereas the MoE baseline appears to receive one pass. With widths sampled between 0.25 and 1.0, this represents substantial additional training computation. Training FLOPs, wall-clock cost, and a compute-matched MoE baseline are absent, so full-width quality gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed structure.

The evidence lacks uncertainty estimates. No number of seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, despite several small differences in Table 1 and evaluation on WSC with only 273 examples. Table 2 reports only one selected MoSE operating point per task, without uniform-width controls or a clear budget-selection protocol, making downstream claims vulnerable to operating-point selection.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the headline results. The abstract's code link is blank; random seeds and several implementation details are missing; the unusual batch notation in Table 3 is unexplained; runtime precision, batch size, sequence/context conditions, and kernel implementation are unspecified; and the DeepSeek-V2-Lite experiment omits the exact checkpoint, adaptation duration, schedule, and treatment of its SwiGLU/shared-expert architecture.

The runtime evidence is too limited to establish deployment efficiency. Figure 16 uses only a few operating points and does not state essential measurement conditions. Dynamic per-token widths may introduce grouping, padding, kernel-launch, and load-imbalance costs that FLOP counts do not capture, particularly in distributed MoE serving.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the architecture is a fairly direct combination of established slimmable/nested networks and MoE routing. Router-probability-based allocation is sensible, but the claimed learned allocation is both low-dimensional and currently underspecified at its most important technical step.

The limitations discussion is only one short paragraph and identifies chiefly the absence of frontier-scale pretraining. strengths: The paper presents a useful and conceptually appealing combination of sparse MoE routing with nested, slimmable expert FFNs. Separating expert selection from expert capacity is reasonably original and enables multiple inference operating points from one checkpoint.

The empirical scope is broad: several GPT-style scales and routing configurations, up to a 2.5B model trained on 50B tokens, finer-grained E64A8/E128A8 settings, downstream zero-shot tasks, and continual-pretraining adaptation of DeepSeek-V2-Lite. The reported compute-quality improvements are generally consistent across these settings.

The paper includes helpful ablations comparing uniform, fixed probability-based, shared-parameter TTT, and layer-wise TTT allocation. It also provides FLOP breakdowns, training curves, routing diagnostics, and limited latency/throughput measurements rather than reporting perplexity alone.

Presentation is mostly clear and the central architecture is easy to understand. The limitations and impact sections appropriately acknowledge the absence of frontier-scale from-scratch validation and the possibility of width-dependent safety behavior; these honest disclosures should not be penalized.
weaknesses: The central test-time-training procedure is not technically specified in a sound, reproducible way. Expert width determines an integer slice through m(w)=ceil(4dw), and the experiments further discretize widths in increments of 0.05. Consequently, the language-model loss is piecewise constant and non-differentiable with respect to gamma, yet the appendix says gamma is optimized with SGD. No straight-through estimator, soft-mask relaxation, derivative-free procedure, or other gradient mechanism is described. Since most headline gains rely on TTT, this is a material gap rather than a minor implementation detail.

The claimed fixed-budget allocation is also underspecified. Equation 10 makes widths sum to Gamma before projection, but clipping each width to [w_min,w_max] generally changes that sum; no redistribution or constrained projection algorithm is given. Indeed, at Gamma=|S|, any nonuniform allocation necessarily clips the largest width and leaves unused budget. This complicates the interpretation and reproduction of matched-compute comparisons.

Training comparisons do not control or report total training compute. Each MoSE iteration performs a full-width pass plus a sampled-width pass, whereas the MoE baseline appears to perform one pass, while both are compared using nominal token counts. Exact training FLOPs, wall-clock cost, and compute-matched baselines are needed to establish whether inference savings compensate for the additional training expenditure.

Practical runtime evidence is substantially narrower than the FLOP claims. Dynamic per-token widths can cause batching, grouping, and kernel-efficiency overheads, but runtime is reported only for small E8A2/E64A8 settings without sufficient benchmarking details or measurements for the 2.5B and DeepSeek models. Thus the strong deployment-efficiency framing is supported mainly by analytical FLOPs rather than end-to-end latency at the most relevant scales.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code link is blank; random seeds and uncertainty estimates are absent; tokenizer and evaluation-harness details are missing; the calibration/evaluation split is not precisely identified; and the DeepSeek adaptation lacks sufficient information about architecture-specific expert slicing, token budget, and optimization schedule. The lack of error bars is especially relevant for small evaluations such as the 273-example WSC set and modest downstream differences.

Empirical baselines are limited to vanilla MoE and variants of the proposed model. Related elastic/slimmable approaches are discussed but not compared experimentally, making the magnitude of the advance over the closest alternatives unclear. The limitations section also omits the important training-cost and dynamic-kernel-efficiency limitations. Ethical discussion is otherwise adequate.
